title: Olbers' Paradox: Why Is the Sky Dark at Night?
question: If the universe is infinite and full of stars, why does the night sky look mostly dark instead of blazing with light in every direction?
summary: A seemingly trivial observation—that the night sky is dark—turns out to rule out an infinite, static, eternal universe, and points instead toward a universe with a finite age and an expanding, cooling afterglow we now call the cosmic microwave background.
content:
Step outside on a clear night and look up. The sky between the stars is dark. This seems too obvious to be a scientific mystery—but for centuries it was one of the most productive puzzles in cosmology, quietly implying that the universe must have either an edge, an age, or a death, long before anyone had direct evidence for any of the three.

The Core Paradox

If the universe is infinite, static, and eternal, and stars are scattered through it roughly evenly, then in every direction you look, your line of sight should eventually hit a star—no matter how far away. Distant stars appear dimmer, but there are proportionally more of them at greater distances, and those two effects cancel out exactly: a shell of stars at twice the distance is four times dimmer individually, but there are four times as many stars in that shell. The conclusion, worked out clearly by Heinrich Olbers in 1823 (though Kepler and others had puzzled at versions of it earlier) is startling: an infinite, static, evenly-populated universe should have a night sky as bright as the surface of a star, everywhere, all the time. It plainly does not. Something in the premises must be false.

The Wrong Answers That Seemed Right

The first tempting explanation is dust: maybe interstellar clouds block the light of distant stars. This fails on inspection—over infinite time, dust would absorb enough radiation to heat up and re-radiate just as brightly as the stars behind it. A second guess is that the universe is simply too sparse, with too much empty space between stars. But sparseness alone doesn't help either: over a truly infinite universe, sparseness just pushes the average stellar surface further away without preventing every line of sight from eventually terminating on one.

The Real Answer: A Universe With a Birthday

The actual resolution is that the universe is not infinitely old and static. It began roughly 13.8 billion years ago, so light from stars farther than about 13.8 billion light-years away simply hasn't had time to reach us yet—our observable universe is a finite sphere, not an infinite static field. Worse for the old picture, the universe is expanding, and the light from the most distant visible objects has been stretched by that expansion into infrared and microwave wavelengths, invisible to the naked eye. The universe's afterglow really is everywhere in the sky, at every point—it's the cosmic microwave background, and it is extraordinarily uniform. We just can't see it, because our eyes aren't built to detect microwaves.

What This Tells Us About the Universe

Olbers' Paradox is a rare case where a purely qualitative observation—the sky is dark at night—constrains cosmology as forcefully as any telescope measurement. A dark night sky is, logically, evidence that the universe had a beginning, or is finite, or both. Long before redshift surveys or the discovery of the cosmic microwave background in 1965 confirmed the Big Bang model observationally, the mere darkness of the night sky was already incompatible with an eternal, unchanging, infinite universe of stars.

Lingering Puzzles

The paradox is resolved for stars, but its logic resurfaces in subtler forms. Why does the universe have a low-entropy, ordered beginning at all, rather than starting (or having always existed) in the featureless, maximum-disorder state thermodynamics seems to favor? And what does the eventual heat death of the universe—an end state of maximum entropy and darkness—say about whether "the sky is dark" is a temporary cosmic accident or an inevitability arriving from the other direction too?

perspectives.title: Cosmology Perspective
perspectives.description: The finite age of the universe means only a finite volume of space is observable; light from beyond roughly 13.8 billion light-years hasn't reached Earth yet, resolving the paradox directly.

perspectives.title: History of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: Olbers' Paradox shows how a simple everyday observation, rigorously reasoned through, can rule out entire cosmological models decades before direct observational evidence becomes available.

perspectives.title: Physics (Thermodynamics) Perspective
perspectives.description: An infinite, eternal, static starfield would violate energy conservation intuitions by implying infinite accumulated radiation; the universe's finite age and expansion prevent this from ever occurring.

perspectives.title: Philosophy Perspective
perspectives.description: The paradox is a case study in how background assumptions (infinite, static, eternal) can each seem individually reasonable while jointly producing an observably false prediction, forcing a reexamination of which assumption to abandon.

openQuestions: Why did the universe begin in a highly ordered, low-entropy state rather than a disordered one, given that disorder is statistically far more probable?
Will the night sky's darkness persist indefinitely, or does the long-term fate of the universe (heat death, or a Big Rip) eventually change what "dark" even means?
How much of the total universe lies forever beyond our observable horizon, unreachable even in principle?
Could there be other quiet, everyday observations, as simple as a dark sky, that are secretly ruling out major cosmological models today without anyone yet noticing?
